Worthy Is the Lamb
wẽr´thy ĭz thē lăm
n. phrase (the song of heaven in Revelation 5; the sevenfold ascription to the Lamb that was slain)
Greek arnion, a little lamb — the diminutive, used twenty-nine times in Revelation and once elsewhere, and axios, worthy, of due weight. The One who governs the book is named by the smallest and most defenceless word available.

Biblical Definition

Worthy is the Lamb is sung by every creature: “Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing” (Rev 5:12). The ground of the worthiness is given first: “Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood” (Rev 5:9). The Lamb is seen before He is sung: “in the midst of the throne… stood a Lamb as it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes” (Rev 5:6). The title was given at the Jordan: “Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). And Isaiah saw the slaughter: “he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth” (Isa 53:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines lamb as the young of the sheep kind, and, in Scripture, the Lamb of God, the Savior Jesus Christ, who was offered as a sacrifice for sins; and worthy as deserving, having merit, possessing worth or excellence of qualities.

LAMB, n. The young of the sheep kind.

2. The Lamb of God, in Scripture, the Savior Jesus Christ, who was typified by the paschal lamb.

Behold the Lamb of God, who taketh away the sin of the world. John 1.

WORTHY, a. Deserving; such as merits; having worth or excellence; as a worthy man.

2. Possessing worth or excellence of qualities; virtuous; estimable.

Key Scripture

Rev 5:12 — "Saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing."

Rev 5:9 — "And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation;"

Rev 5:6 — "And I beheld, and, lo, in the midst of the throne and of the four beasts, and in the midst of the elders, stood a Lamb as it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent forth into all the earth."

John 1:29 — "The next day John seeth Jesus coming unto him, and saith, Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world."

Isa 53:7 — "He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth."

Modern Corruption

The Lamb is sung as gentle and nothing more, and the Lamb of Revelation opens the seals, has seven horns, and has a wrath the kings flee from.

expand to see more

The word is a diminutive — a little lamb — and the figure in Revelation 5:6 is as it had been slain, standing with the marks of its death on it. That is the meekness the church rightly sings. But the same verse gives the Lamb seven horns and seven eyes, which are complete power and complete sight; the Lamb opens the seals that release judgment; and in chapter 6 the kings of the earth call on the mountains to hide them from the wrath of the Lamb. A Lamb with wrath is a deliberate paradox and the book will not let either half go. The slain One is the One in authority, and the authority is exercised by the slain One.

The song grounds the worthiness in a purchase, and the grounding matters for theology. Chapter 4 sings Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things — the Creator's worthiness. Chapter 5 sings Thou art worthy to take the book… for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood — the Redeemer's. The Lamb is not worthy merely because He is divine; He is worthy to open history because He paid for it. That is why 5:12 heaps up seven things — power, riches, wisdom, strength, honour, glory, blessing — the number of completeness, as if the singers were emptying the vocabulary.

Isaiah 53:7 and John 1:29 stand behind the song and supply its silence. The lamb brought to the slaughter openeth not his mouth; the Lamb of God taketh away the sin of the world, in a present tense that the church has been living inside ever since. Revelation 5 is the only place in Scripture where every creature in heaven and on earth and under the sea is heard at once, and what they agree on is the worth of the One who did not defend Himself. The church's whole liturgy, every Lord's day, is a rehearsal of that verse by a choir still learning its part.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek arnion (G721), a little lamb; axios (G514), worthy, of weight; esphagmenon (G4969), slain, slaughtered; Hebrew seh (H7716), a lamb, one of the flock.

expand to see more

Greek arnion (G721) — little lamb; Revelation 5:6–13, 6:16, 7:17, 21:23, 22:3; elsewhere only John 21:15.

Greek hos esphagmenon (G4969) — as it had been slain; Revelation 5:6, 5:9, 5:12, 13:8.

Hebrew kasseh lattebach (H7716, H2874) — as a lamb to the slaughter; Isaiah 53:7, Jeremiah 11:19.

Usage

"“A Lamb as it had been slain, having seven horns” — the paradox the book keeps."

"“For thou wast slain” — the Redeemer's worthiness, after the Creator's."

"“Power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing” — seven."
